opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most exciting directions for us right now. If you look at where JEPA started, with I-JEPA on images and then V-JEPA on video, the core idea has always been the same: you learn by predicting missing or future information in an abstract representation space, rather than reconstructing every pixel. That lets the model focus on what's actually predictable and meaningful about the world, and ignore the stuff that's essentially noise, like the exact texture of leaves blowing in the wind.

But a world model trained only on passive video is fundamentally limited. It can learn a lot about intuitive physics, how objects move, persist, interact, but it's an observer. It never learns the consequences of its own actions. So one of the most important signals to bring in is action. Once you condition the predictor on actions, you're no longer just asking "what happens next?" You're asking "what happens next if I do this?" That's what makes the model useful for planning, and that's the step we took with action-conditioned versions of V-JEPA, where you can do zero-shot planning for robotic manipulation by rolling out the model in latent space and searching for actions that reach a goal.

Beyond actions, there are other modalities that carry complementary information. Audio tells you about contact events and materials that are hard to see. Proprioception and touch tell you about forces, and depth gives you geometric structure. Language is interesting too, not necessarily as the primary training signal, but as a way to specify goals or ground abstract concepts. The nice thing about the JEPA framework is that it's fairly agnostic to the input. You encode each signal into a shared representation space, and the prediction objective encourages the model to find the latent structure that ties them together. If you can predict what something will sound like from how it looks, or how it'll feel from how it moves, that's strong evidence you've captured something real about the underlying physical state.

There are real challenges. Different signals operate at different time scales and resolutions, and you have to be careful the model doesn't latch onto one easy modality and ignore the others. Representation collapse is always a concern in joint-embedding methods, and adding modalities gives the model more ways to find shortcuts. So a lot of the work is in designing the masking and prediction tasks so the model is forced to integrate information across signals rather than treating them independently.

But fundamentally, I think the richer and more grounded the signals are, especially ones tied to interaction, the closer we get to a world model that supports reasoning and planning rather than just recognition. That's really the goal: not a model that describes the world, but one that can anticipate it and act within it.

r001.rationale: It describes JEPA’s prediction objective but does not identify fully unsupervised learning as a reason it can scale.

r002.rationale: It says combining signals can reveal shared latent structure and help the model capture the underlying physical state, supporting more meaningful predictions.

r003.rationale: It does not propose that multiple modalities enable predictions over longer horizons.

r004.rationale: It frames the goal as a world model that supports reasoning and planning, beyond recognition or video encoding alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that the world model is really only as good as the information it has access to about the world. With the early JEPA work, we were mostly focused on vision, first images and then video, and the idea there was: can we learn to predict missing parts of a scene in an abstract representation space rather than at the pixel level? And that turns out to give you representations that capture things like object permanence, basic physics, how things move and interact over time.

But if you think about how a child learns, they're not just passively watching. They're getting proprioceptive feedback, they're hearing sounds, they're taking actions and seeing what happens. Each of those signals constrains the model in a different way. Vision tells you about the state of the world, but action tells you about causality, about what happens when you intervene. Audio can disambiguate things that are visually ambiguous, like whether a collision actually made contact. Language gives you a kind of compressed, high-level abstraction of what's going on, labels for concepts that would otherwise take a lot of experience to discover on your own.

So when we incorporate more of these signals, the hope is that the latent space becomes richer and more grounded. Predictions in that space should start to reflect not just "what does the next frame look like" but "what will happen if I do this," and that's really the core of what a world model needs to be useful for planning. We've seen a bit of this already with the action-conditioned work, where you can take a JEPA that's been pretrained on video and then post-train it on a relatively small amount of interaction data, and suddenly you can use it to plan robot manipulation in a zero-shot way. That's a nice proof point that the additional signal doesn't have to be massive, it just has to be the right kind of information to fill in the gaps.

The challenge, honestly, is doing this without collapsing everything into one modality's view of the world. You want these signals to complement each other, to let the model learn the shared structure across them, rather than just having language dominate because it's the easiest to predict. So a lot of the architectural work is about how you fuse these representations, how you decide what to predict from what, and how you keep the objective focused on the predictable, meaningful parts of the world and not the noise.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adding signals and interaction data, but does not identify fully unsupervised learning as a reason JEPA can scale.

r002.rationale: It says multiple signals can make the latent space richer and grounded, with language providing high-level abstractions and audio resolving visual ambiguity.

r003.rationale: It describes action-conditioned planning, but does not propose that multimodal inputs enable predictions over longer horizons.

r004.rationale: It frames the goal as a useful world model for planning, extending beyond predicting video frames or learning a video representation.

astra-6.text:
I think the intuition is that different signals give you complementary information about the same underlying world. If you’re learning from video, you can observe how things change, but you don’t necessarily know what caused that change. If you also have actions, you can start learning how an action affects what happens next. Audio can provide information about events that might be difficult to infer visually.

With JEPA, the idea is to predict in a representation space, so you don’t have to model every detail of each signal. You want to capture the information that helps you understand and predict what’s happening. Incorporating more signals should help constrain those representations and make them more useful.

The hope is that this takes us toward a model that can do more than recognize a situation—it can anticipate how that situation might evolve, including in response to an action. But simply adding modalities isn’t enough; the learning objective has to encourage the model to capture those relationships.

r002.rationale: It says multiple signals provide complementary information and constrain representations, but does not clearly say they make JEPA’s predictions more semantic.

r003.rationale: It discusses anticipating how a situation evolves, but does not mention predicting over longer horizons.

r004.rationale: It frames the goal as a model that understands and anticipates how the world changes, including in response to actions, beyond simply recognizing a situation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the motivation is that different signals give you complementary information about the world. Video tells you how things move and interact, audio can tell you about events that you might not see, and actions tell you how you can influence what happens next. If you can learn to predict across those signals in a shared representation space, the hope is that you capture more of the underlying structure of the world.

And with JEPA, the idea is that you don’t have to predict every detail of those signals. You want to predict the aspects that are informative and predictable, while abstracting away details that don’t matter. Actions are particularly interesting because you can move from predicting what happens next to predicting what happens next if I do something. That’s the kind of world model you could ultimately use for planning.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention fully unsupervised learning or scalability.

r002.rationale: It says multiple signals can reveal underlying world structure, but does not clearly say they make JEPA’s predictions more semantic.

r003.rationale: It discusses predicting what happens next and planning, but does not say multiple modalities enable predictions over longer horizons.

r004.rationale: It frames learning across signals as capturing the world’s underlying structure and describes an action-conditioned world model for planning.
